## DTW Alignment

> is based on distance metrics

### DTW alignment between two time series

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Depict DTW of a pair of time series

``` python

def depict_DTW(
    x1:ndarray,
    x2:ndarray, # Time series where the first dimension is time and the second dimension are the features.
    dist:Callable=euclidean, # Distance metric function to use for DTW.
    radius:int=1, # Radius parameter for the FastDTW algorithm.
):

```

*Use `fastdtw` to visualize the DTW alignment between two time series.*

<div>

> **FastDTW: radius value**
>
> The `radius` parameter controls how wide the refinement window is
> around the projected DTW path in FastDTW.  
> It must be a **non‑negative integer** (`0, 1, 2, …`). Larger values
> improve accuracy at the cost of speed.
>
> <table>
> <colgroup>
> <col style="width: 36%" />
> <col style="width: 42%" />
> <col style="width: 21%" />
> </colgroup>
> <thead>
> <tr>
> <th><code>radius</code> value</th>
> <th>Interpretation</th>
> <th>Effect</th>
> </tr>
> </thead>
> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><code>0</code></td>
> <td>Follow projected path exactly; no refinement</td>
> <td>Fastest, least accurate</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>1</code></td>
> <td>Slight refinement around the path</td>
> <td>Still fast; modest accuracy gain</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>2</code></td>
> <td>Balanced refinement window</td>
> <td>Good trade‑off between speed and accuracy</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>≥ 5</code></td>
> <td>Wide refinement window</td>
> <td>Much slower; very close to exact DTW</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>

</div>

<div>

> **radius value**
>
> Applies to `fastdtw` only.

</div>

### DTW alignment between multiple time series

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Depict distance matrix as a heatmap

``` python

def plot_dm_heatmap(
    ts, # Array of shape (n_samples, n_features, n_timesteps).
    alignment_type:str='fastdtw', # Type of alignment method to use. Options:
'dcor' or DTW type ('fastdtw', 'tslearn_dtw', 'soft_dtw', 'soft_dtw_div').
    gamma:int=1, # Smoothing parameter for Soft-DTW (only used for DTW-based alignment types):
- Small gamma → behaves like classic DTW (hard minimum)
- Large gamma → smoother, more diffused alignment
    dist:function=euclidean, # Distance metric function used inside DTW. Only applies when alignment_type='fastdtw'.
Ignored for 'tslearn_dtw' (uses euclidean), 'soft_dtw'/'soft_dtw_div' (use squared euclidean),
and 'dcor'.
    p:int=3, # Parameter for Minkowski distance (if used). Only applies to DTW-based alignment types.
    radius:int=1, # Radius parameter for the FastDTW algorithm. Only applies when alignment_type='fastdtw'.
    normalize:NoneType=None, # Normalization method for the distance matrix.
Options: 'max', 'minmax', 'z-score', 'l1', 'l2', 'softmax', 'sym', 'log', 'none'.
    n_jobs:int=4, # Number of parallel jobs.
    labels:NoneType=None, # Labels for the time series. If None, defaults to TS0, TS1, ...
    title:str='Distance Matrix Heatmap', # Title of the plot.
    color_continuous_scale:str='Viridis', # Colormap for the heatmap.
    base_size:int=20, # Base pixel size per time series (controls figure dimensions).
): # Displays an interactive Plotly heatmap.

```

*Visualize a DTW distance matrix as an interactive Plotly heatmap with
hover tooltips.* The distance matrix is computed using either distance
correlation (dcor) or a DTW-based method depending on the selected
alignment type.

> <td><code>tslearn_dtw</code></td>
> <td><code>tslearn_dtw(ts1, ts2)</code></td>
> <td>Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)</td>
> <td><span
> class="math display">DTW(<em>X</em>, <em>Y</em>) = min<sub><em>π</em></sub>∑<sub>(<em>i</em>, <em>j</em>) ∈ <em>π</em></sub>∥<em>X</em><sub><em>i</em></sub> − <em>Y</em><sub><em>j</em></sub>∥</span></td>
> <td>Exact DTW; dynamic programming; <span
> class="math inline"><em>O</em>(<em>n</em><sup>2</sup>)</span>.</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>fastdtw</code></td>

> <td>Linear‑time, linear‑space approximation; very fast.</td>
> </tr>

> <td><code>tslearn_soft_dtw(ts1, ts2, gamma)</code></td>
> <td>Soft‑DTW</td>
> <td><span class="math display">$$\text{SoftDTW}_\gamma(X,Y) = -\gamma
> \log \sum_{\pi} e^{-\frac{1}{\gamma}
> \sum_{(i,j)\in\pi}\|X_i-Y_j\|}$$</span></td>
> <td>Differentiable relaxation of DTW; controlled by
> <code>gamma</code>.</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>soft_dtw_div</code></td>
> <td><code>soft_dtw_divergence(ts1, ts2, gamma)</code></td>
> <td>Soft‑DTW Divergence</td>
> <td><span class="math display">$$D(X,Y) = \mathrm{SoftDTW}(X,Y) -
> \tfrac{1}{2}(\mathrm{SoftDTW}(X,X) +
> \mathrm{SoftDTW}(Y,Y))$$</span></td>
> <td>Proper divergence; symmetric; <span
> class="math inline"> ≥ 0</span>.</td>
> </tr>

> **Matrix Normalization Methods — API Summary**
>
> <table>
> <colgroup>
> <col style="width: 17%" />
> <col style="width: 34%" />
> <col style="width: 13%" />
> <col style="width: 10%" />
> <col style="width: 14%" />
> <col style="width: 9%" />
> </colgroup>
> <thead>
> <tr>
> <th><code>normalize</code> value</th>
> <th>Meaning / Transformation</th>
> <th>Equation</th>
> <th>Scope</th>
> <th>Strengths</th>
> <th>Notes</th>
> </tr>
> </thead>
> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><code>max</code></td>
> <td>Global max normalization</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>M</em> ← <em>M</em>/max (∥<em>M</em>∥)</span></td>
> <td>Whole matrix</td>
> <td>Simple global scaling; preserves sign</td>
> <td>Sensitive to outliers; collapses if max is 0</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>minmax</code></td>
> <td>Min–max scaling to <span class="math inline">[0, 1]</span></td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$M \leftarrow \dfrac{M - \min(M)}{\max(M)
> - \min(M)}$</span></td>
> <td>Whole matrix</td>
> <td>Uniform scaling; preserves relative ordering</td>
> <td>If all values equal → returns zeros</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>z-score</code></td>
> <td>Standardization (zero mean, unit variance)</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$M \leftarrow \dfrac{M -
> \mu}{\sigma}$</span></td>
> <td>Whole matrix</td>
> <td>Centers + scales; good for Gaussian‑like data</td>
> <td>If <span class="math inline"><em>σ</em> = 0</span> → returns
> zeros</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>l1</code></td>
> <td>Row‑wise L1 normalization</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$M_{i,:} \leftarrow \dfrac{M_{i,:}}{\sum_j
> \|M_{i,j}\|}$</span></td>
> <td>Row‑wise</td>
> <td>Produces rows summing to 1; good for sparse data</td>
> <td>Zero rows remain zero (safe handling)</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>l2</code></td>
> <td>Row‑wise L2 normalization</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$M_{i,:} \leftarrow
> \dfrac{M_{i,:}}{\sqrt{\sum_j M_{i,j}^2}}$</span></td>
> <td>Row‑wise</td>
> <td>Normalizes direction; common in embeddings</td>
> <td>Zero rows remain zero (safe handling)</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>softmax</code></td>
> <td>Row‑wise softmax (probabilities)</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$M_{i,j} \leftarrow
> \dfrac{e^{M_{i,j}}}{\sum_k e^{M_{i,k}}}$</span></td>
> <td>Row‑wise</td>
> <td>Converts rows into probability distributions</td>
> <td>Uses max‑shift for numerical stability</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>sym</code></td>
> <td>Symmetric graph normalization</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>M</em> ← <em>D</em><sup>−1/2</sup> <em>M</em> <em>D</em><sup>−1/2</sup></span>
> where <span
> class="math inline"><em>D</em><sub><em>i</em><em>i</em></sub> = ∑<sub><em>j</em></sub><em>M</em><sub><em>i</em><em>j</em></sub></span></td>
> <td>Whole matrix</td>
> <td>Standard in spectral graph theory; stabilizes adjacency
> matrices</td>
> <td>Adds <span class="math inline">1<em>e</em>−8</span> to avoid
> division by zero</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>log</code></td>
> <td>Logarithmic transform</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>M</em> ← log (1 + <em>M</em>)</span></td>
> <td>Element‑wise</td>
> <td>Compresses large values; reduces skew</td>
> <td>Requires non‑negative input for meaningful interpretation</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>None</code></td>
> <td>No normalization</td>
> <td>—</td>
> <td>—</td>
> <td>Leaves matrix unchanged</td>
> <td>Useful for debugging or raw comparisons</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>

</div>

<div>

> **gamma value**
>
> The **gamma (*γ*)** parameter controls how quickly similarity decays
> with distance in the Gaussian/RBF kernel. It effectively sets the
> *locality scale* of the embedding: small *γ* captures global
> structure, large *γ* emphasizes local neighborhoods. Here, **d**
> denotes a characteristic distance scale, e.g. the **median** of all
> pairwise distances in the distance matrix.
>
> <table>
> <colgroup>
> <col style="width: 31%" />
> <col style="width: 11%" />
> <col style="width: 24%" />
> <col style="width: 20%" />
> <col style="width: 11%" />
> </colgroup>
> <thead>
> <tr>
> <th><span class="math inline"><em>γ</em></span> value (relative to
> distance scale)</th>
> <th>Kernel Width</th>
> <th>Effect on Similarity Matrix</th>
> <th>Effect on 3D Embedding</th>
> <th>When to Use</th>
> </tr>
> </thead>
> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Very small</strong> (<span
> class="math inline"><em>γ</em> ≈ 0.001/<em>d</em><sup>2</sup></span>)</td>
> <td>Very wide</td>
> <td>Most distances map to high similarity (matrix almost uniform)</td>
> <td>Embedding collapses; points cluster together</td>
> <td>When distances are extremely noisy; rarely useful</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Small</strong> (<span
> class="math inline"><em>γ</em> ≈ 0.01/<em>d</em><sup>2</sup></span>)</td>
> <td>Wide</td>
> <td>Slow decay; far points still moderately similar</td>
> <td>Smooth, global structure; weak cluster separation</td>
> <td>When you want global geometry preserved</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Medium</strong> (<span
> class="math inline"><em>γ</em> ≈ 0.1/<em>d</em><sup>2</sup></span>)</td>
> <td>Balanced</td>
> <td>Reasonable decay; neighbors clearly more similar</td>
> <td>Balanced embedding: clusters visible, global shape preserved</td>
> <td><strong>Good default</strong> when scale is unknown</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Large</strong> (<span
> class="math inline"><em>γ</em> ≈ 1/<em>d</em><sup>2</sup></span>)</td>
> <td>Narrow</td>
> <td>Only close neighbors have high similarity</td>
> <td>Strong cluster separation; global shape distorted</td>
> <td>When clusters matter more than global layout</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Very large</strong> (<span
> class="math inline"><em>γ</em> ≥ 10/<em>d</em><sup>2</sup></span>)</td>
> <td>Very narrow</td>
> <td>Almost all similarities ≈ 0 except identical points</td>
> <td>Embedding becomes noisy; overfitting to local noise</td>
> <td>Only for extremely tight local structure</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>

</div>

> **gamma value**
>
> Applies to `soft_dtw` only.

### DTW alignment geometry

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Distance matrix projection using a dimensionality reduction method

``` python

def plot_dm_projection(
    ts:VAR_POSITIONAL, # Arrays of shape (n_samples, n_features, n_timesteps)
    alignment_type:str='fastdtw', # Type of alignment method to use: 'dcor' or DTW type ('fastdtw', 'tslearn_dtw', 'soft_dtw', 'soft_dtw_div').
    gamma:int=1, # smoothing parameter (for soft_dtw only):
    Small gamma → behaves more like classic DTW (hard minimum)
    Large gamma → smoother, more diffused alignment (less sensitive to exact path)
    0.01 Very close to DTW:     Precise alignment
    1.0 Balanced smoothing:     Most common default
    10.0 Very smooth: Robust to noise, good for optimization
    dist:function=euclidean, # Distance metric function to use for DTW is implicitly euclidean. Only applies for alignment_type='fastdtw'.
    p:int=3, # Parameter for Minkowski distance (if used).
    radius:int=1, # Radius parameter for the FastDTW algorithm.
    projection:str='mds', # Distance Matrix MDS Projection or PCA or TSNE
    transformation:str='gauss', # Method to transform distances into similarities for PCA.
    Options: 'gauss', 'invert', 'minmax'
    normalize:NoneType=None, # Normalization method to apply to the similarity matrix.
    Options: 'max', 'minmax', 'z-score', 'l1', 'l2', 'softmax', 'sym', 'none'
    n_jobs:int=4, # number of jobs for parallel execution
    labels:NoneType=None, # labels for each time series.
    title:str='Distance Matrix Projection', # plot title
    color:str='blue', # color for points
    dimensions:int=2, # 2 or 3 for projection
):

```

*Visualize distance matrix using MDS, TSNE, or PCA (2D or 3D projection)
with Plotly.* The distance matrix is calculated using distance
correlation (dcor) or a DTW method.

<div>

> **Similarity Transformations for PCA- Summary Table**
>
> <table>
> <colgroup>
> <col style="width: 17%" />
> <col style="width: 19%" />
> <col style="width: 23%" />
> <col style="width: 23%" />
> <col style="width: 17%" />
> </colgroup>
> <thead>
> <tr>
> <th><code>transformation</code> value</th>
> <th>Formula</th>
> <th>Intuition</th>
> <th>Strengths</th>
> <th>Notes</th>
> </tr>
> </thead>
> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Gaussian (RBF) Similarity</strong></td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$K_{ij} =
> \exp\!\left(-\frac{D_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$</span></td>
> <td>Nearby points get high similarity; far points decay smoothly</td>
> <td>Handles nonlinear structure; tunable locality via <span
> class="math inline"><em>σ</em></span></td>
> <td>Most common kernel for PCA on distance‑based data</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Inverse Distance Similarity</strong></td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$K_{ij} = \frac{1}{1 +
> D_{ij}}$</span></td>
> <td>Similarity decreases monotonically with distance</td>
> <td>Simple, bounded, interpretable</td>
> <td>Good when distances vary widely</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>Min‑Max Normalized Similarity</strong></td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$K_{ij} = 1 - \frac{D_{ij} -
> D_{\min}}{D_{\max} - D_{\min}}$</span></td>
> <td>Linearly maps distances to <span
> class="math inline">[0, 1]</span></td>
> <td>Preserves rank; easy to visualize</td>
> <td>Useful when PCA expects normalized inputs</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>

</div>

> **transformation value**
>
> Applies to PCA only.

</div>

#### Intrinsic dimensionality of a distance matrix via singular value decomposition (SVD)

> Compute Singular Value Decomposition of a Distance Matrix

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### svd_dmatrix

``` python

def svd_dmatrix(
    ts, # Arrays of shape (n_samples, n_timesteps) or (n_samples, n_features, n_timesteps).
    alignment_type:str='fastdtw', # Type of alignment method to use ('dcor', 'fastdtw', 'tslearn_dtw', 'soft_dtw', 'soft_dtw_div').
    gamma:int=1, # smoothing parameter (for soft_dtw only):
    Small gamma → behaves more like classic DTW (hard minimum)
    Large gamma → smoother, more diffused alignment (less sensitive to exact path)
    0.01 Very close to DTW:     Precise alignment
    1.0 Balanced smoothing:     Most common default
    10.0 Very smooth: Robust to noise, good for optimization
    dist:function=euclidean, # Distance metric function to use for DTW (only for fastdtw).
    p:int=3, # Parameter for Minkowski distance (if used).
    radius:int=1, # Radius parameter for the FastDTW algorithm.
    transformation:str='gauss', # Method to transform distances into similarities.
    Options: 'gauss', 'invert', 'minmax'
    normalize:NoneType=None, # Normalization method to apply to the similarity matrix.
    Options: 'max', 'minmax', 'z-score', 'l1', 'l2', 'softmax', 'sym', 'none'
    n_jobs:int=4, # number of jobs for parallel execution
): # U: Left singular vectors
S: Singular values (1D array)
Vt: Transpose of right singular vectors

```

*Compute the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of a similarity matrix
derived from time series distances.* The distance matrix is calculated
using distance correlation (dcor) or a DTW method.

## Classification Accuracy

> of a binary classification problem. A class contains landmark
> embeddings (rows in a DTW distance matrix) of time series that are
> synchronized, i.e., belong to the same segment the underlying
> `Datasource` object.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Calculate and store

``` python

def calc_dtw_accuracy(
    Xopera0, Xopera1, dirname, # Directory in which the results Excel file will be stored.
    dtw_type:str='fastdtw', # DTW method to use ('fastdtw', 'tslearn_dtw', 'soft_dtw').
    normalize:bool=False, # Whether to normalize the data ('minmax' or 'meanvar').
    radius:int=1, # Radius parameter for fastdtw.
    feature:NoneType=None, # Feature index to include in the output filename.
    random_states:int=1, # Number of random train–test splits to evaluate.
)->Path: # Path to the Excel file containing the computed accuracy results.
The file is guaranteed to exist upon return.
Path = ROOT/dirname/acc_summ.xlsx or acc_summ_{feature}.xlsx if feature is specified.

```

*Compute classification accuracies across multiple classifiers and
DTW-based embeddings, and write the aggregated results to an Excel
file.*

The output directory is created if missing. The Excel file is always
written before the function returns and contains: - a combined summary
of all classifiers, - metadata describing the evaluation setup, -
per-classifier accuracy summaries and split-level results.

> <tr>
> <td><code>euclidean</code></td>
> <td>Standard L2 distance</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$d(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i -
> y_i)^2}$</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>

> class="math inline"><em>p</em> = 2</span></td>

> <tr>
> <td><code>nan_euclidean</code></td>
> <td>NaN‑aware Euclidean distance</td>
> <td>Same as Euclidean, computed only over non‑NaN dimensions</td>

> <td>Generalized Lp distance</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>d</em>(<em>x</em>, <em>y</em>) = (∑<sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<em>x</em><sub><em>i</em></sub> − <em>y</em><sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<sup><em>p</em></sup>)<sup>1/<em>p</em></sup></span></td>
> <td>Raw features; requires <code>p</code></td>
> <td>Flexible family including L1, L2, L∞</td>

> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>cosine</code></td>
> <td>Cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity)</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$d(x,y) = 1 - \frac{x \cdot
> y}{\|x\|\|y\|}$</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>
> <td>Good for directional / high‑dimensional data</td>
> <td>Scale‑invariant; undefined for zero vectors</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>l1</code></td>
> <td>Manhattan (cityblock) distance</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>d</em>(<em>x</em>, <em>y</em>) = ∑<sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<em>x</em><sub><em>i</em></sub> − <em>y</em><sub><em>i</em></sub>∥</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>

#### Classifier Variant Naming Convention

The return value is a dictionary mapping **classifier variants** to
accuracy scores.

Each key is constructed as: `<classifier_name>_`

where:

- KNN expands over **distance metrics**
- SVM expands over **kernel types**
- Other classifiers have a **single variant** (no suffix)

dictionary may look like:

``` python
{
    "knn_euclidean": 0.83,
    "knn_cosine": 0.79,
    "knn_precomputed": 0.91,
    "svm_linear": 0.88,
    "svm_rbf": 0.92,
    "randf": 0.90,
    "rotf": 0.94,
    "shapelet_rotationforest": 0.96,
}
```

### Retrieve and visualize

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### depict_accuracy

``` python

def depict_accuracy(
    dirname, # Directory containing the accuracy summary files.
    features:NoneType=None, # If None or empty, a single file `acc_summ.xlsx` is loaded.
If a list is provided, each feature name `f` triggers loading
`acc_summ_{f}.xlsx`.
    filename:str='acc_summ.xlsx', # Filename used when `features` is None. Default is `"acc_summ.xlsx"`.
    statistics:str='median', # Statistic to extract from the summary tables. Options: `"median"`, `"mean"`, `"std"`, `"iqr"` (interquartile range).
    dtw_filter:NoneType=None, # Optional filter restricting which DTW variants are included.
    columns_filter:NoneType=None, # Optional filter restricting which classifier columns are included.
    verbose:bool=False, # If True, prints additional information during loading and filtering.
): # The constructed accuracy plot.

```

*Plot classifier accuracy curves from one or multiple accuracy summary
files.*

This function loads accuracy summary tables (in the format produced by
the pipeline’s `acc_summ*.xlsx` files), reshapes them into a long
format, and produces publication‑quality accuracy plots. When multiple
features or DTW variants are present, the function delegates all color,
dash, and marker assignments to the external `style_registry` module to
ensure consistent, reproducible styling across figures.
